abstract: SUMMARY Stem cell-based replacement therapies hold the promise to restore function of damaged or degenerated tissue such as the pancreatic islets in people with type 1 diabetes. Wide application of these therapies requires overcoming the fundamental roadblock of immune rejection. To address this issue, we use genetic engineering to create human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) in which the majority of the polymorphic human leukocyte antigens (HLAs), the main drivers of allogeneic rejection, are deleted. We retain the common HLA class I allele HLA-A2 and less polymorphic HLA-E/F/G to allow immune surveillance and inhibition of natural killer (NK) cells. We employ a combination of in vitro assays and humanized mouse models to demonstrate that these gene manipulations significantly reduce NK cell activity and T-cell-mediated alloimmune response against hPSC-derived islet cells. In summary, our approach produces hypoimmunogenic hPSCs that can be readily matched with recipients to avoid alloimmune rejection.

Cas9 RNP and the cell solution were added to a Nucleocuvette (Lonza) and nucleofection was carried out using the setting CA137 on the Amaxa 4D-Nucleofector. Cells were replated on MEFs in hESC maintenance media supplemented with ROCK inhibitor. Four days after nucleofection, cells were either collected for genomic DNA extraction or stained for FACS sorting.
Flow cytometry and sorting of edited hPSCs
Cells that were subjected to transfection or nucleofection were dissociated using TrypLE Select (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and resuspended in sterile FACS buffer (1% FBS + 2mM EDTA in PBS -Mg/-Ca). Cells were stained with primary antibodies (details are provided in
key resources table
) for 30–60 min at 4°C. Stained cells were washed with FACS buffer and resuspended in FACS buffer containing DAPI. Cells were either analyzed on a BD LSR Fortessa or sorted using a BD FACS Aria II. Sorted cells were collected in hPSC maintenance media supplemented with ROCK inhibitor and PenStrep and re-seeded at low density (~15–25,000 cells per 10-cm plate) onto multidrug-resistant irradiated DR4 MEFs (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Sorted cells were cultured in hESC maintenance media supplemented with ROCK inhibitor until they formed clonal colonies. Individual colonies were manually picked and replated into individual wells of 96-well plates pre-seeded with DR4 MEFs. Clonal lines were further expanded, screened by flow cytometry, and sequenced to identify correctly targeted clones. For flow cytometry screening, hPSCs from clonal lines were seeded on a separate 96-well plate and treated with 50 ng/mL IFNγ (PeproTech) for 48–72h prior to analysis.

Differentiation into pancreatic cells

6

The plates were incubated at 37°C and 5% CO2 on an orbital shaker set at 100 rpm to induce 3D sphere formation. After 24 hours, the spheres were differentiated as previously described (
Nair et al., 2019b
). Spheres were collected in 50 mL tubes, allowed to settle by gravity, washed once with PBS, and resuspended in day 1 differentiation media. The resuspended spheres were distributed into fresh 6-well suspension plates for a final volume of 5.5 mL of day 1 media per well. Until day 3, spheres were fed daily by removing 5 mL of the media and replenishing with 5.5 ml. From days 4 to 20, 5 mL media was removed daily and 5 mL of fresh media was added. Media compositions are as follows: Day 1: RPMI (GIBCO) containing 0.2% FBS, 1:5,000 ITS (GIBCO), 100 ng/ml activin A and 50 ng/ml WNT3a (R&D Systems). Day 8: DMEM with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27, 3 nM TTNPB and 50 ng/ml EGF (R&D Systems). Day 9–11: DMEM with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27, 50 ng/ml EGF and 50 ng/ml KGF. Day 12+: DMEM with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27, 1:100 Glutamax (GIBCO), 1:100 NEAA (GIBCO), 10 μm ALKi II (Axxora), 500 nM LDN-193189 (Stemgent), 1 μm Xxi (Millipore), 1 μM T3 (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 mM vitamin C, 1 mM N-acetyl cysteine (Sigma-Aldrich),10 μM zinc sulfate (Sigma-Aldrich) and 10 μg/ml of heparin sulfate.

Dynamic perifusion assay for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion
Dynamic glucose-stimulated insulin secretion was performed using a perifusion system (Biorep technologies) as previously described (
Nair et al., 2019b
). For each sample, one hundred sorted clusters were handpicked and placed on filters in plastic chambers that were maintained under temperature and CO
2
controlled conditions. After an initial 1–2 hour preincubation period in 2.8 mM glucose in KRB buffer, chambers were sequentially perifused at a flow rate of 100 μl/min with 2.8 mM glucose for 20 min and 20 mM glucose for 30 min. Flow-through was collected over the course of the experiment, and insulin concentrations in the supernatant were determined using an ultrasensitive insulin ELISA kit (STELLUX Chemi Human C-peptide ELISA from Alpco).
Immunostaining
Differentiated β-like clusters were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min at room temperature, washed with PBS, and stored at 4°C until ready for processing. β-like clusters were first embedded in 2% agar, followed by dehydration, paraffin embedding, and sectioning at 5 μm thickness. Paraffin-embedded sections were rehydrated in an ethanol gradient followed by incubation in slow boiling antigen retrieval Citra Solution (Biogenex). Spleen tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 2–4h, washed with PBS, followed by overnight incubation with 30% (w/v) sucrose (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS. Tissues were embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Tissue-Tek) and stored at −80°C before sectioning on a cryostat (Leica). Slides were briefly rehydrated in PBS before staining. For immunofluorescence staining, tissue was permeabilized and blocked in CAS block (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with 0.2% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) for at least 20 min, followed by primary antibody staining at 4°C overnight. Sections were washed with PBS-Tween 0.1% prior to secondary antibody staining performed at room temperature for 1h. Sections were washed again with PBS-Tween 0.1% before mounting with ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were acquired on an SP5 confocal microscope (Leica). Antibody details are provided in
key resources table
.
Quantitative real-time PCR
Samples harvested at indicated stages of differentiation were homogenized in RLT buffer (QIAGEN). RNA was extracted and purified using RNeasy Mini/Micro kits (QIAGEN). cDNA was synthesized with iScript (Biorad). qPCR was performed using SYBR green on Biorad CFX Connect Real-Time PCR Detection System. Assay was performed using diluted cDNA samples and primers against genes of interest and GAPDH as internal control. Primer details are listed in
key resources table
.
Intracellular flow cytometry
Differentiated clusters were dissociated into single cells using Accumax (Thermo Fisher Scientific), fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized, and stained for various intracellular markers as described previously (
Russ et al., 2015
). The anti-human C-peptide and glucagon antibodies were conjugated in-house using the Molecular Probes Antibody Labeling Kits according to manufacturer’s instructions. Antibody details are listed in
key resources table
. Data were analyzed using FlowJo software.
HLA-E surface expression in the presence of signal peptide
β-like cells were cultured for 24h in the presence of 100 μM of a synthetic peptide derived from HLA-A2 leader sequence (residues 3–11 – VMAPRTLVL) (GeneScript) added directly to the differentiation media. Clusters were dissociated into single cells using Accumax prior to cell surface staining with an HLA-E antibody (
key resources table
) for 60 min at 7–8°C. Stained cells were washed with FACS buffer, resuspended in FACS buffer containing DAPI, and analyzed on a BD LSR Fortessa or LSR II.
Isolation of human PBMC
Human PBMC were isolated from fresh leukapheresis packs obtained from healthy donors (StemCell Technologies). Demographics and HLA class I typing for each donor is presented in
Table S2
. Processing was done on the day of collection and was started by performing an initial white blood cell count. Cells diluted 1:4 with D-PBS without added calcium or magnesium were then overlaid onto Ficoll-Paque Plus density media (GE Healthcare), and the cells were centrifuged for 20 min at 1000xg, at room temperature with no brake. After this density gradient separation, PBMC were harvested and washed with D-PBS followed by centrifugation at 450xg for 10 min at room temperature with brake. A red blood cells lysis step was performed using ACK lysis buffer (Lonza) followed by another wash with D-PBS. Cells were then counted and assessed for viability using a Vi-Cell XR automated cell counter (Beckman Coulter) before being cryopreserved in 90% fetal bovine serum + 10% dimethylsulfoxide.

200,000 human PBMC were pre-incubated with 5 ng/mL IL-12 (PeproTech) in NK assay media (RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, glutamax, non-essential amino acids, 1 mM HEPES, 1 mM pyruvate, and Penicillin Streptomycin) for 24 hours. β-like clusters from WT, HLA-ABC
null

R
lines were either left untreated or pretreated with 50 ng/mL IFNγ (PeproTech) for 24h prior to dissociation and incubation with PBMC. 50,000 target cells were added to the PBMC and incubated for 2 hours under 5% (v/v) CO
2
. The data was acquired on a BD LSR Fortessa, LSR II, or FACSAria (Becton Dickinson). Antibody details are provided in
key resources table
.
Transplantation studies
The day before transplantation, 40–60×10
6
human PBMC were administered intravenously via retro-orbital injection. The next day, approximately 2–3×10
6
β-like cells left untreated or pretreated with 50 ng/mL IFNγ (PeproTech) for 24h were transplanted in the spleen of NSG or NSG-MHC
null
mice. Spleens were harvested at indicated time points for immunostaining and flow cytometric analysis of splenocytes.
Lentiviral infection
hPSCs differentiated up to day 14–15 were dissociated to single cells using Accumax. Digested cells were filtered on a 0.4 μm strainer and reaggregated in a suspension plate in the presence of lentiviral particles carrying a luciferase transgene (kindly provided by Dr. Audrey Hendley). Cells were reaggregated in differentiation media containing 10 μM of the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Tocris) and 6 μg/ml of polybrene (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Bioluminescence imaging
Mice transplanted with luciferase-expressing cells were injected intraperitoneally (IP) with 15 mg/mL D-luciferin solution (Goldbio Biotechnology) before imaging on a Xenogen IVIS 200 imaging system (Perkin Elmer). Signals were acquired and analyzed using the Living Image analysis software (Xenogen Corp). Regions of interests (ROIs) of the same size were manually drawn and bioluminescence was quantified as total flux (photons/sec). Background bioluminescence (determined using control mice not transplanted with hPSCs) was substracted from total flux values. Identical protocol was strictly followed for sequential imaging of the same mice to ensure comparability of assay performance over time.
Estimation of HLA allele frequency
The Allele Frequency Net Database (
www.allelefrequencies.net
) was used to estimate the frequency of HLA-A*02 in different populations. Data for HLA-A*02 allele frequency in all populations and all regions of the world in studies that contained more than 1000 subjects was extracted. This has resulted in a report that included 102 studies and 3,467,432 individuals from Europe, USA, South America, Asia and Africa (
Table S1
). This report shows that the HLA-A2 allele is present at an average frequency of 27.2% with standard deviation of 3.4%. In addition, 26 of these studies reported the % individuals that have this allele, which is 48.2% on average with a standard deviation of 5.8%.

cells were sorted on a BD FACS Aria II at low flow rates. Sorted cells were reaggregated in Aggrewell-400 plates according to the manufacturer’s instructions (StemCell Technologies). Cells were seeded in reaggregation media (CMRL containing 10% FBS, 1:100 Glutamax (GIBCO), 1:100 NEAA (GIBCO), 10 μm ALKi II (Axxora), 0.5 mM vitamin C, 1 μM T3 (Sigma-Aldrich), 1 mM N-acetyl Cysteine (Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM zinc sulfate (Sigma-Aldrich) and 10 μg/ml of heparin sulfate) supplemented with 10 μM of the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Tocris) and Penicillin Streptomycin (Corning). The seeding density was adjusted to have 1,000 cells per cluster. Two to three days later, reaggregated clusters were transferred to ultra-low-attachment plates (VWR catalog #657185) and placed on an orbital shaker set at 100 rpm. Clusters were further cultured for up to 15 days. Media was changed every third day following reaggregation.
Dynamic perifusion assay for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion
Dynamic glucose-stimulated insulin secretion was performed using a perifusion system (Biorep technologies) as previously described (
Nair et al., 2019b
). For each sample, one hundred sorted clusters were handpicked and placed on filters in plastic chambers that were maintained under temperature and CO
2
controlled conditions. After an initial 1–2 hour preincubation period in 2.8 mM glucose in KRB buffer, chambers were sequentially perifused at a flow rate of 100 μl/min with 2.8 mM glucose for 20 min and 20 mM glucose for 30 min. Flow-through was collected over the course of the experiment, and insulin concentrations in the supernatant were determined using an ultrasensitive insulin ELISA kit (STELLUX Chemi Human C-peptide ELISA from Alpco).
Immunostaining
Differentiated β-like clusters were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min at room temperature, washed with PBS, and stored at 4°C until ready for processing. β-like clusters were first embedded in 2% agar, followed by dehydration, paraffin embedding, and sectioning at 5 μm thickness. Paraffin-embedded sections were rehydrated in an ethanol gradient followed by incubation in slow boiling antigen retrieval Citra Solution (Biogenex). Spleen tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 2–4h, washed with PBS, followed by overnight incubation with 30% (w/v) sucrose (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS. Tissues were embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Tissue-Tek) and stored at −80°C before sectioning on a cryostat (Leica). Slides were briefly rehydrated in PBS before staining. For immunofluorescence staining, tissue was permeabilized and blocked in CAS block (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with 0.2% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) for at least 20 min, followed by primary antibody staining at 4°C overnight. Sections were washed with PBS-Tween 0.1% prior to secondary antibody staining performed at room temperature for 1h. Sections were washed again with PBS-Tween 0.1% before mounting with ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were acquired on an SP5 confocal microscope (Leica). Antibody details are provided in
key resources table
.
Quantitative real-time PCR
Samples harvested at indicated stages of differentiation were homogenized in RLT buffer (QIAGEN). RNA was extracted and purified using RNeasy Mini/Micro kits (QIAGEN). cDNA was synthesized with iScript (Biorad). qPCR was performed using SYBR green on Biorad CFX Connect Real-Time PCR Detection System. Assay was performed using diluted cDNA samples and primers against genes of interest and GAPDH as internal control. Primer details are listed in
key resources table
.
Intracellular flow cytometry
Differentiated clusters were dissociated into single cells using Accumax (Thermo Fisher Scientific), fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized, and stained for various intracellular markers as described previously (
Russ et al., 2015
). The anti-human C-peptide and glucagon antibodies were conjugated in-house using the Molecular Probes Antibody Labeling Kits according to manufacturer’s instructions. Antibody details are listed in
key resources table
. Data were analyzed using FlowJo software.
HLA-E surface expression in the presence of signal peptide
β-like cells were cultured for 24h in the presence of 100 μM of a synthetic peptide derived from HLA-A2 leader sequence (residues 3–11 – VMAPRTLVL) (GeneScript) added directly to the differentiation media. Clusters were dissociated into single cells using Accumax prior to cell surface staining with an HLA-E antibody (
key resources table
) for 60 min at 7–8°C. Stained cells were washed with FACS buffer, resuspended in FACS buffer containing DAPI, and analyzed on a BD LSR Fortessa or LSR II.
Isolation of human PBMC
Human PBMC were isolated from fresh leukapheresis packs obtained from healthy donors (StemCell Technologies). Demographics and HLA class I typing for each donor is presented in
Table S2
. Processing was done on the day of collection and was started by performing an initial white blood cell count. Cells diluted 1:4 with D-PBS without added calcium or magnesium were then overlaid onto Ficoll-Paque Plus density media (GE Healthcare), and the cells were centrifuged for 20 min at 1000xg, at room temperature with no brake. After this density gradient separation, PBMC were harvested and washed with D-PBS followed by centrifugation at 450xg for 10 min at room temperature with brake. A red blood cells lysis step was performed using ACK lysis buffer (Lonza) followed by another wash with D-PBS. Cells were then counted and assessed for viability using a Vi-Cell XR automated cell counter (Beckman Coulter) before being cryopreserved in 90% fetal bovine serum + 10% dimethylsulfoxide.
NK cell degranulation assay
200,000 human PBMC were pre-incubated with 5 ng/mL IL-12 (PeproTech) in NK assay media (RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, glutamax, non-essential amino acids, 1 mM HEPES, 1 mM pyruvate, and Penicillin Streptomycin) for 24 hours. β-like clusters from WT, HLA-ABC
null
, or HLA-A2
R
lines were either left untreated or pretreated with 50 ng/mL IFNγ (PeproTech) for 24h prior to dissociation and incubation with PBMC. 50,000 target cells were added to the PBMC and incubated for 2 hours under 5% (v/v) CO
2
. The data was acquired on a BD LSR Fortessa, LSR II, or FACSAria (Becton Dickinson). Antibody details are provided in
key resources table
.
Transplantation studies
The day before transplantation, 40–60×10
6
human PBMC were administered intravenously via retro-orbital injection. The next day, approximately 2–3×10
6
β-like cells left untreated or pretreated with 50 ng/mL IFNγ (PeproTech) for 24h were transplanted in the spleen of NSG or NSG-MHC
null
mice. Spleens were harvested at indicated time points for immunostaining and flow cytometric analysis of splenocytes.
Lentiviral infection
hPSCs differentiated up to day 14–15 were dissociated to single cells using Accumax. Digested cells were filtered on a 0.4 μm strainer and reaggregated in a suspension plate in the presence of lentiviral particles carrying a luciferase transgene (kindly provided by Dr. Audrey Hendley). Cells were reaggregated in differentiation media containing 10 μM of the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Tocris) and 6 μg/ml of polybrene (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Bioluminescence imaging
Mice transplanted with luciferase-expressing cells were injected intraperitoneally (IP) with 15 mg/mL D-luciferin solution (Goldbio Biotechnology) before imaging on a Xenogen IVIS 200 imaging system (Perkin Elmer). Signals were acquired and analyzed using the Living Image analysis software (Xenogen Corp). Regions of interests (ROIs) of the same size were manually drawn and bioluminescence was quantified as total flux (photons/sec). Background bioluminescence (determined using control mice not transplanted with hPSCs) was substracted from total flux values. Identical protocol was strictly followed for sequential imaging of the same mice to ensure comparability of assay performance over time.
Estimation of HLA allele frequency
The Allele Frequency Net Database (
www.allelefrequencies.net
) was used to estimate the frequency of HLA-A*02 in different populations. Data for HLA-A*02 allele frequency in all populations and all regions of the world in studies that contained more than 1000 subjects was extracted. This has resulted in a report that included 102 studies and 3,467,432 individuals from Europe, USA, South America, Asia and Africa (
Table S1
). This report shows that the HLA-A2 allele is present at an average frequency of 27.2% with standard deviation of 3.4%. In addition, 26 of these studies reported the % individuals that have this allele, which is 48.2% on average with a standard deviation of 5.8%.

Supplementary Material
Supplementary material
Supplemental information can be found online at
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2021.109538
.
body:
INTRODUCTION
Transplantation of pancreatic β cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) has emerged as a promising approach for the treatment of type 1 diabetes (T1D). Remarkable progress has been made with regard to generation of functional β cells from hPSCs, which could soon replace human islets as a source of insulin-producing cells (
Hogrebe et al., 2020
;
Nair et al., 2019b
;
Pagliuca et al., 2014
;
Rezania et al., 2014
;
Russ et al., 2015
;
Velazco-Cruz et al., 2019
). However, successful clinical translation of stem cell therapies requires addressing the barrier of immune rejection due to alloimmune and islet-specific autoimmune responses against β cells present in patients with diabetes. Several approaches are envisioned to circumvent this problem, including global immunosuppression using drugs currently given to transplant recipients, induction of immune tolerance, shielding of cells in immunoprotective encapsulation devices, and utilization of highly efficient gene editing tools to reduce the immunogenicity of hPSCs (
Lanza et al., 2019
;
Sneddon et al., 2018
).
The main drivers of the immune rejection of transplanted allogeneic tissue are the highly polymorphic classical human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C. These HLAs are expressed on all nucleated cells and present antigens to CD8
+
T cells, while HLA class II molecules (HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR) are expressed mostly on antigen-presenting cells to activate CD4
+
T cells. Expression of class II molecules can be induced on other cell types in inflammatory conditions. Notably, in the context of T1D, β cells react to inflammation by hyperexpression of HLAs, increasing their immunogenicity and likelihood of rejection (
Pujol-Borrell et al., 1987
;
Foulis and Farquharson, 1986
;
Russell et al., 2019
). Possible approaches to diminish the strength of the immune response toward pancreatic islet stem cell grafts thus include the editing of hPSCs to eliminate the expression of all HLA class I molecules through deletion of β2-microglobulin (
Deuse et al., 2019
;
Mattapally et al., 2018
;
Riolobos et al., 2013
), a molecule required for folding and stable expression of these proteins on the cell surface. Alternatively, hPSCs can be edited to only express less polymorphic alleles via targeted deletion of specific HLAs. While both strategies permit easier matching of stem cell derivatives with recipients, only the preservation of common alleles ensures immune surveillance of the graft should cells become infected with viruses or form tumors. In addition, retaining less polymorphic genes could help prevent natural killer (NK)-cell-mediated killing of the graft, which can be triggered by the absence of HLA class I expression on the cells. For example, retaining non-classical HLA-E, HLA-F, and HLA-G, in combination with the highly prevalent HLA class I molecule HLA-A2, known to present numerous peptides derived from viruses and tumors (
Gotch et al., 1987
;
He et al., 2019
), could inhibit NK cells while ensuring immune surveillance of the graft. Importantly, the HLA-A*02 allele has a very high frequency among several ethnic groups, including ~50% of white and Asian populations (
Gonzalez-Galarza et al., 2011
) (
Table S1
), hence facilitating matching with potential recipients.
Here, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to delete all highly polymorphic HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C class I genes except HLA-A2 from hPSCs and eliminated the class II transactivator (CIITA), the master transactivator of HLA class II expression (
Chang et al., 1996
). We validated that genetic engineering did not impair the ability of the hPSCs to differentiate into insulin-producing cells. Importantly, we showed that this HLA reduction strategy is effective at inhibiting NK cell activation while protecting β-like cells from T-cell-mediated rejection in a humanized mouse model. By retaining only HLA-A2 and less polymorphic HLA alleles, we therefore generated hPSCs that have decreased immunogenicity with the hope that they can be transplanted in HLA-A2
+
recipients without the need for long-term global immunosuppression.
RESULTS
Generation of HLA-ABC
null
and HLA-A2
R
cell lines
To create cells that are less immunogenic, the CRISPR-Cas9 technology was used to abrogate expression of the classical HLA class I genes
HLA-A
,
HLA-B
, and
HLA-C
and/or the HLA class II activator
CIITA
in MEL1 INS
GFP/W
, a human pluripotent stem cell line in which a GFP protein was knocked into one allele of the endogenous insulin locus (
Micallef et al., 2012
). MEL1 INS
GFP/W
HLA typing for class I alleles is presented in
Table S2
. Cells with complete loss of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C expression (HLA-ABC
null
hPSCs) were first generated to serve as a control for our assays. To increase the efficiency of targeting, inducible Cas9 expression cassettes were introduced into the
AAVS1
locus of the cells using an established method (
González et al., 2014
) to create an iCas9 line (
Figures 1A
and
S1A
). Guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting coding regions of the
HLA-A
,
HLA-B
, and
HLA-C
genes were designed to specifically bind to both alleles of each gene (
Table S3
). The efficiency of these gRNAs was assessed by transfecting them into doxycycline-treated iCas9 cells followed by tracking of indels by decomposition (TIDE) analysis (
Brinkman et al., 2014
) (
Figure S1B
). The gRNAs with the highest efficiency (gRNAs A2, B4, and C3) were selected to generate the HLA-ABC
null
line (
Figure 1B
, black bars). While the efficiency of editing was reduced when combining all three gRNAs (
Figure 1B
, gray bars), staining of transfected cells with a pan-HLA class I antibody and sorting of cells with negative expression increased the proportion of successfully edited cells (
Figure 1B
, white bars). A total of 60 clonal lines from the HLA-ABC
−
sorted cells were established and screened by flow cytometry for negative expression of HLA class I (
Figure 1A
). Three clones with negative expression of HLA-A2, HLA-A24, and HLA-B were identified and further sequenced to confirm the presence of indels in both alleles of
HLA-A
,
HLA-B
, and
HLA-C
(
Figure S1D
). To functionally assess the loss of HLA expression in the established HLA-ABC
null
clonal lines, we performed flow cytometric analysis of cells treated with interferon gamma (IFNγ), a pro-inflammatory cytokine known to induce HLA class I expression. As shown in
Figures 1C
and
1D
, IFNγ treatment increased expression of HLA class I by more than 10-fold in wild-type (WT) but only marginally in HLA-ABC
null
cells while HLA-A2, HLA-A24, and HLA-B were not detected in HLA-ABC
null
cells. The low level of expression of HLA class I in HLA-ABC
null
cells is possibly due to induction of non-classical alleles such as HLA-E, HLA-F, and HLA-G, which are also recognized by the pan-HLA class I W6/32 antibody (
Rouas-Freiss et al., 1997
). In summary, by combining gRNAs for each of the
HLA-A
,
HLA-B
, and
HLA-C
genes, we were able to obtain clones with complete loss of all three genes.
To preserve the immune surveillance competence of the cells, we next generated hPSCs that had lost expression of all classical HLA class I genes but retained expression of HLA-A2 (HLA-A2
R
hPSCs). In addition, expression of HLA class II alleles was blocked by targeting the
CIITA
locus coding for an essential transcriptional activator of HLA class II expression. To create the HLA-A2
R
line, WT MEL1 INS
GFP/W
cells were electroporated with Cas9/gRNAs ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) (
Figure 1E
, step 1). This targeting strategy was selected over the iCas9 method used to generate HLA-ABC
null
cells, since it allows introduction of a luciferase construct in the
AAVS1
locus, a modification not possible in the iCas9 line that already carries transgenes in both alleles of this locus (
González et al., 2014
). A first round of editing that included gRNAs targeting
HLA-A
,
HLA-B
,
HLA-C
, and
CIITA
was performed, followed by sorting of cells with low levels of HLA class I but normal expression of HLA-A2 (
Figure 1E
, step 2). Clonal lines established from sorted cells were screened to identify cells that had lost expression of HLA-A24, but not HLA-A2 (
Figure 1E
, step 3). These selected clones were electroporated again to generate indels in both alleles of
HLA-B
and
HLA-C
, as well as
CIITA
(
Figure 1E
, step 4). Since the sequences of HLA class I genes are highly homologous, we selected gRNAs that were complementary to
HLA-B
or
HLA-C
but had many mismatches with
HLA-A
to avoid introducing new indels in
HLA-A2
(
Figure S1C
). Clonal lines were screened by flow cytometry to select cells that had lost expression of HLA-B but retained expression of HLA-A2 (
Figure 1E
, step 5). These clones were then sequenced to screen for additional mutations in
HLA-C
and
CIITA
, leading to the identification of cells with mutations in all classical HLA class I genes but
HLA-A2
as well as indels in both alleles of
CIITA
(HLA-A2
R
) (
Figure S1E
). Retention of HLA-A2 expression as well as loss of HLA-A24 and HLA-B in HLA-A2
R
hPSCs was confirmed by flow cytometry (
Figures 1F
and
1G
). Analysis of pluripotent cultures confirmed that engineered cells express similar levels of the pluripotency markers
POU5F1
(also known as
OCT4
), NANOG, and SOX2 as the parental line (
Figures S1F
–
S1H
). In summary, our multi-pronged CRISPR-based approach generated cells lacking expression of HLA-A24, HLA-B, HLA-C, and CTIIA while maintaining expression of HLA-A2 as a mediator of immune surveillance.
Characterization of β-like cells derived from immunoengineered clones
To assess the differentiation potential of immunoengineered clones, we used an established multi-stage protocol to generate pancreatic β-like cells (
Figure 2A
) (
Nair et al., 2019b
). The efficiency of differentiation for the first stage (definitive endoderm) was similar among WT, HLA-ABC
null
, and HLA-A2
R
cells, with all lines generating more than 90% SOX17
+
FOXA2
+
cells (data not shown). All cell lines produced >70% PDX1
+
/NKX6.1
+
pancreatic endoderm cells (data not shown) as well as similar percentages of β-like cells co-positive for C-peptide and the key β cell markers PDX1, NKX6.1, NKX2.2, and NEUROD1 (
Figures 2B
,
2C
,
S2A
, and
S2B
). Immunofluorescence staining and gene expression analysis of β-like cells also confirmed similar levels of expression of chromogranin A (
CHGA
), MAFB, and NKX2.2 in all cell lines (
Figures S2C
and
S2D
). Finally, we sorted GFP
+
insulin-expressing cells to generate enriched β clusters (eBCs) from the three cell lines (
Nair et al., 2019b
) and evaluated their physiological properties to ensure that the gene editing process did not result in defects in the insulin secretion or glucose transport machinery that would impair cell function. We performed a dynamic glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) assay using a perfusion system. As shown in
Figure 2D
, eBCs generated from the three cell lines showed a similar increase in insulin secretion in response to glucose, indicating that the genome engineering process did not impact the function of hPSC-derived β cells. Taken together, our data indicate that the immunoengineering process did not affect the potential of CRISPR-edited lines to form definitive endoderm as well as subsequently differentiate into functional pancreatic β cells.
Next, to determine the level of expression of HLA class I on WT, HLA-ABC
null
, and HLA-A2
R
β cells, we performed flow cytometric analysis using a pan-HLA class I antibody. A subset of cells was also treated with IFNγ for 24 h to assess induction of HLA class I when β cells are exposed to this pro-inflammatory cytokine. HLA expression in WT and HLA-A2
R
cells was rapidly induced on both insulin-positive and insulin-negative cells after IFNγ treatment of β-like cells or eBCs (
Figures 2E
and
S2E
). While overall levels of HLA class I proteins were lower in HLA-A2
R
compared to WT cells, expression of HLA-A2 was similar (
Figures 2F
,
2G
, and
S2E
). As expected, HLA-ABC
null
cells did not upregulate any HLA class I molecules (
Figures 2E
–
2G
and
S2E
). In addition, cells were stained for HLA-E, a non-classical HLA class I allele that can inhibit NK cell activity (
Borrego et al., 1998
;
Braud et al., 1998a
). Importantly, while expression of HLA-E was not detected in HLA-ABC
null
cells, both WT and HLA-A2
R
cells upregulated its expression in response to IFNγ (
Figures 2H
and
2I
). These results suggest that ablation of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C led to a loss of HLA-E expression, likely due to the requirement for signal peptides from other HLA class I molecules to enable its surface expression (
Borrego et al., 1998
;
Braud et al., 1998a
). In contrast, retention of HLA-A2 was sufficient to restore HLA-E expression possibly due to the presence of HLA-A2-derived signal peptides. To verify this hypothesis, β-like cells were treated with IFNγ in the presence of a synthetic peptide derived from the HLA-A2 leader sequence (
Braud et al., 1998b
). As shown in
Figures 2H
and
2I
, incubation with this signal peptide rescued HLA-E expression in ABC
null
cells, supporting the idea that the presence of HLA-A2 promotes surface of expression of HLA-E in HLA-A2
R
cells through binding of its signal peptide. Finally, since IFNγ exposure has been shown to induce expression of the immunomodulatory molecule PD-L1 on β cells (
Osum et al., 2018
), we quantified its expression in β-like cells following a 24 h incubation with 50 ng/mL IFNγ. This treatment led to upregulation of PD-L1 in all three cell lines (
Figures S2F
and
S2G
). In summary, immunoengineered clones differ in their HLA expression profile but retain the ability to upregulate immunomodulatory molecules like PD-L1 in the presence of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IFNγ.
Retaining expression of HLA-A2 in combination with non-classical HLA class I alleles reduces NK cell activation
Given that HLA class I molecules can reduce NK-mediated cytolysis through binding to inhibitory receptors, complete ablation of HLA class I expression may make the cells more vulnerable to NK targeting. To assess if the deletions in HLA-ABC
null
and HLA-A2
R
cells lead to increased NK cell activation, we performed an
in vitro
degranulation assay using human NK cells among peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). This flow cytometric assay measures NK cell responses by quantifying cell surface expression of CD107a (also known as LAMP-1), a protein found in intracellular vesicles in resting NK cells but transferred to the cell surface when NK cells are activated to release cytotoxic granules (
Bryceson et al., 2010
). We thus measured its surface expression on CD56
+
CD3
−
NK cells from peripheral blood of normal donors after 2 h of stimulation with WT, HLA-ABC
null
, or HLA-A2
R
β-like cells. The day before the assay, β-like cells were left untreated or pretreated with IFNγ for 24 h to increase expression of all HLA class I genes while PBMCs were pre-incubated with interleukin-12 (IL-12) to enhance NK cell activity (
Figure 3A
). Upregulation of CD107a surface expression on NK cells was detected when PBMCs were exposed to untreated β-like cells derived from all three cell lines, suggesting that the level of HLA expression in the absence of IFNγ is too low to efficiently inhibit activation (
Figures 3B
,
3C
, and
S3A
). In contrast, IFNγ treatment of WT and HLA-A2
R
β-like cells led to a significant reduction in CD107a surface expression, while treatment of HLA-ABC
null
cells did not, indicating that these cells lack the ability to upregulate HLAs that can inhibit NK cells (
Figures 3B
,
3C
, and
S3A
). While HLA-A2 itself does not have the ability to suppress NK cells, its presence promoted surface expression of HLA-E after IFNγ treatment (
Figures 2H
and
2I
), likely accounting for the increased inhibition of NK cells by HLA-A2
R
cells when compared to HLA-ABC
null
cells. However, HLA-A2
R
cells were not able to inhibit activation to the same extent as WT cells (
Figures 3B
,
3C
, and
S3A
). Since the inhibitory receptor bound by HLA-E (CD94/NKG2A) is only expressed by a subset of NK cells (
Figure S3B
), the higher level of activation in the presence of HLA-A2
R
cells is likely due to lack of inhibition of NKG2A
−
cells. Taken together, these results indicate that retaining expression of HLA-A2, in combination with non-classical alleles like HLA-E, reduced the activation of a subset of NK cells.
Deletion of all but a single classical HLA class I is effective at protecting β-like cells from T-cell-mediated rejection
Since the main drivers of allogeneic responses are HLA molecules, we expect that deleting most of the genes in the HLA-A2
R
line will reduce rejection in an allogeneic model. To test this hypothesis, transcription activator-like effector nuclease (TALEN) technology was used to introduce a constitutive firefly luciferase construct in the transcriptionally active
AAVS1
locus of WT and HLA-A2
R
lines so that survival of transplanted cells could be monitored noninvasively using bioluminescence imaging (
Figure 4A
). The day before transplantation, immunodeficient NOD
scid
gamma (NSG) mice or a strain of NSG mice with both murine major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and II genes deleted (NSG-MHC
null
mice) (
Brehm et al., 2019
) were reconstituted with PBMCs obtained from HLA-A2
+
donors (
Figure 4B
). The NSG-MHC
null
strain was created to address a major limitation of the NSG model, which develops acute xenogeneic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) when injected with human PBMCs due to T cell recognition of murine MHC. Deletion of murine MHC in NSG-MHC
null
mice renders mice more resistant to GVHD, thus making long-term experiments possible. To increase the chances that the human immune cells traffic to the stem cell graft, β-like cells were injected in the spleen, a site where human T cells reliably traffic. In addition, stem cells differentiated to the β-like stage were left untreated or pretreated with IFNγ for 24 h prior to transplantation to assess the impact of higher levels of HLA expression on the immunogenicity of the cells (
Figure 4B
). Transplanted mice were monitored weekly using noninvasive bioluminescence imaging to determine if there was a decline in the mass of grafted cells due to immune destruction. Notably, only β-like cells that were treated with IFNγ were reliably rejected in this model (
Figure 4C
). The pre-treatment step was therefore included when assessing the immunogenicity of cells derived from edited lines.
As shown in
Figures 4D
,
4E
,
S4A
, and
S4B
, the total cell mass was reduced significantly in WT grafts when compared to HLA-A2
R
grafts starting at 4 weeks post-transplantation in both NSG and NSG-MHC
null
mice. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood and splenocytes confirmed that the absence of rejection observed in HLA-A2
R
grafted mice was not due to lack of engraftment of human cells or T cells in these mice (
Figures S4C
and
S4D
). NK cells were, however, absent 4 weeks post-transplantation (
Figure S4D
). The initial reduction in bioluminescence signal observed in both groups might be due to ischemic injury following transplantation. It has indeed been shown that stem cell-derived β-like cells are susceptible to cell death in the first few weeks post-transplantation until the graft gets vascularized (
Faleo et al., 2017
). Immunofluorescence analysis of harvested grafts confirmed the survival of HLA-A2
+
C-peptide
+
cells in mice transplanted with HLA-A2
R
cells up to 16 weeks post-transplantation (
Figure 4F
). Notably, NSG-MHC
null
mice injected with human PBMCs did not develop lethal GVHD, confirming that this model can be used for long-term
in vivo
studies of human T cell function. In addition, the immunogenicity of HLA-ABC
null
β-like cells was tested after introduction of a luciferase transgene using a lentivirus construct (
Figure S4E
). While a slow decline in luciferase signal was observed in NSG-MHC
null
mice transplanted with HLA-ABC
null
cells, the loss of signal over time is likely not mediated by human immune cells, since a similar decline was seen in mice that did not receive PBMC (
Figure S4F
and
S4G
). In summary, by deleting all classical HLA alleles but HLA-A2, we have generated hPSCs that are less immunogenic when grafted in HLA-A2
+
allogeneic hosts.
DISCUSSION
In this study, we validated that it is feasible to individually inactivate expression of polymorphic HLA class I/II genes in hPSCs without impairing their ability to differentiate into insulin-producing cells. We demonstrated that retention of HLA-A2, in combination with non-classical HLA class I alleles, can reduce activation of NK cells and is also effective at protecting β-like cells from T-cell-mediated rejection in a humanized mouse model.
Other groups have recently reported approaches to create hypoimmunogenic hPSCs by targeting HLAs in combination with retaining one allele of HLA class I (HLA-C) (
Xu et al., 2019
) or overexpression of immunomodulatory molecules (HLA-E, HLA-G, CD47, and/or PD-L1) (
Deuse et al., 2019
;
Gornalusse et al., 2017
;
Han et al., 2019
;
Xu et al., 2019
). Importantly, these methods have been shown to successfully reduce T cell responses without triggering NK cell activation. However, the absence of HLA class I alleles like HLA-A and HLA-B, which have been shown to participate in anti-tumoral and anti-viral responses (
Barnea et al., 2002
;
Crux and Elahi, 2017
;
Gfeller and Bassani-Sternberg, 2018
;
Hunt et al., 1992
), raises concerns about the safety of the cells if they should become malignant or infected. Retention of HLA-A2 expression in stem cell derivatives thus increases the compatibility with potential recipients due to the high prevalence of this allele while reducing the risks associated with immunoengineered cells by preserving the ability of the cells to present antigens that bind to this well-characterized molecule.
In addition, our work showed that, in contrast to complete deletion of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C molecules that leads to loss of HLA-E expression, retention of HLA-A2 was sufficient to reinstate HLA-E expression at the surface of β-like cells. While the gRNAs used to disrupt
HLA-B
and
HLA-C
target sequences downstream of their respective signal peptides (gRNAs B4 and C3 target a region ~300 bp downstream of the signal peptides), the lack of HLA-E expression observed in HLA-ABC
null
cells suggest that signal peptides from truncated HLAs are likely not translated or are not stable enough to promote HLA-E surface expression (
Figure S1D
). Of note, this approach was sufficient to inhibit a subset of NK cells, but retention of additional HLA alleles such as HLA-C or overexpression of an immunomodulatory molecule such as CD47 (
Deuse et al., 2019
;
Han et al., 2019
) might be necessary to suppress NKG2A
−
cells.
When transplanting β cells in patients with T1D, an additional consideration is the possibility for a recurrence of autoimmunity targeting the transplanted β cells that can result in loss of islet graft function. Although deleting most HLAs greatly reduces the number of peptides that can be presented to T cells, there is still a possibility that β cell-specific autoantigens presented by HLA-A2 trigger autoimmune attacks of stem cell-derived β cells. To prevent these autoimmune attacks, it might therefore be necessary to combine the HLA-A2 retention strategy with other approaches that promote local immune regulation. For example, expression of PD-L1 in islets has been shown to delay rejection of transplanted islets (
Fife et al., 2009
;
Gao et al., 2003
;
Keir et al., 2006
;
Wang et al., 2008
) while strategies that promote endogenous regulatory T cells (Treg cells) or direct infusion of Treg cells can reverse autoimmune diabetes and prevent rejection of transplanted islets in mice (
Grinberg-Bleyer et al., 2010
;
Lee et al., 2014
;
Tang et al., 2004
). Stem cell-derived islets could therefore be further modified to enhance immune checkpoints via forced expression of PD-L1 or engineered to secrete factors that promote local accumulation of Treg cells to fend off recurrent autoimmunity. In addition, hPSCs could be exposed to repeated short exposures to IFNγ to induce stable expression of PD-L1, an approach that has been shown to provide immune protection to human islet-like organoids
in vivo
(
Yoshihara et al., 2020
). If successful, these strategies could potentially allow transplantation of human insulin-producing cells into T1D patients without the need for long-term immunosuppression.
In addition to their value in the context of cell therapy, HLA-A2
R
cell lines represent valuable research tools to study interactions between human stem cell derivatives and human immune cells. For example, HLA-A2
R
β cells could be used to assess autoimmune responses to the β cells without the confounding effects of alloimmune response targeting the array of HLA molecules. To study islet autoreactive T cell interaction with HLA-A2
R
β cells, human T cells from an HLA-A2
+
donor can be modified to express a T cell receptor (TCR) that binds islet-specific peptides presented by HLA-A2. These experiments are not possible with hypoimmunogenic cells generated with other strategies like β2-microglobulin ablation, since the resulting cells cannot interact with T cells due to the absence of HLA expression. HLA-A2
R
cell lines will therefore make possible the development of new humanized mouse models to study human autoimmune diseases. One limitation of the study is that all sublines were generated from the same parental line. While our work provides strong evidence that selective deletion of HLA molecules can protect hPSC derivatives from immune rejection, future work will include other hPSC lines completely lacking HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C expression or retaining HLA-A2 to assess their immunogenic potential.
In summary, the experimental strategy described in this study indicates that selective elimination of HLAs reduces the immune response against hPSC-derived islets. These hypoimmunogenic hPSCs can be easily matched with large population of recipients while also retaining immune surveillance competence. This promising approach designed to reduce immune rejection of stem cell derivatives will help address one of the major hurdles facing regenerative medicine.

PPP1R12C
at the
AAVS1

https://www.benchling.com/

Table S3
). The day before gRNA transfection, iCas9 hESCs were treated with doxycycline (1 μg/mL) while ROCK inhibitor (Y-27632 10 μM) was added to the cells a few hours before transfection. Cells were dissociated using TrypLE select and transfected in suspension with gRNAs using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, crRNA and tracrRNA (Dharmacon) mixed at a ratio of 1:1 were annealed by incubation at 37°C for 30 min. 160 ng of the combined gRNAs and Lipofectamine RNAiMAX mixed in Opti-MEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were combined and incubated for 7–8 min at RT. During the incubation, iCas9 hESCs resuspended in hESC maintenance media supplemented with doxycycline and ROCK inhibitor were added to a gelatin-coated 24-well plate (100,000 cells per well). The gRNA/RNAiMAX solution was added dropwise to the iCas9 cells. The next day, MEFs were added to the transfected cells (50,000 cells per well). The cells were cultured in hESC maintenance media supplemented with doxycycline (0.5 μg/mL) until confluent. Upon reaching confluency, cells were dissociated using TrypLE Select (GIBCO) and were either collected for genomic DNA extraction or stained for FACS sorting. Approximately 100,000 cells were used for genomic DNA extraction using QuickExtract solution (Epicenter). Genomic regions flanking the CRISPR target sites were PCR amplified using primers outlined in
Table S4
and the efficiency of genomic editing was determined using TIDE analysis (
Brinkman et al., 2014
).
RNP assembly and nucleofection
Lyophilized crRNAs and tracrRNAs (Dharmacon) were resuspended in RNase-free water at a concentration of 160 μM, and stored in aliquots at −80°C. crRNA and tracrRNA aliquots were thawed, mixed at a ratio of 1:1, and annealed by incubation at 37°C for 30 min to form an 80 μM gRNA solution. Recombinant Cas9 (QB3 Macrolab) was then mixed 1:1 by volume with the 80 μM gRNA (2:1 gRNA to Cas9 molar ratio) at 37°C for 15 min to form an RNP at 20 μM. During the incubation, WT INS
GFP/W
hPSCs were dissociated into single cells using TrypLE Select (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 400,000 cells were resuspended in P3 primary cell solution (Lonza). Cas9 RNP and the cell solution were added to a Nucleocuvette (Lonza) and nucleofection was carried out using the setting CA137 on the Amaxa 4D-Nucleofector. Cells were replated on MEFs in hESC maintenance media supplemented with ROCK inhibitor. Four days after nucleofection, cells were either collected for genomic DNA extraction or stained for FACS sorting.
Flow cytometry and sorting of edited hPSCs
Cells that were subjected to transfection or nucleofection were dissociated using TrypLE Select (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and resuspended in sterile FACS buffer (1% FBS + 2mM EDTA in PBS -Mg/-Ca). Cells were stained with primary antibodies (details are provided in
key resources table
) for 30–60 min at 4°C. Stained cells were washed with FACS buffer and resuspended in FACS buffer containing DAPI. Cells were either analyzed on a BD LSR Fortessa or sorted using a BD FACS Aria II. Sorted cells were collected in hPSC maintenance media supplemented with ROCK inhibitor and PenStrep and re-seeded at low density (~15–25,000 cells per 10-cm plate) onto multidrug-resistant irradiated DR4 MEFs (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Sorted cells were cultured in hESC maintenance media supplemented with ROCK inhibitor until they formed clonal colonies. Individual colonies were manually picked and replated into individual wells of 96-well plates pre-seeded with DR4 MEFs. Clonal lines were further expanded, screened by flow cytometry, and sequenced to identify correctly targeted clones. For flow cytometry screening, hPSCs from clonal lines were seeded on a separate 96-well plate and treated with 50 ng/mL IFNγ (PeproTech) for 48–72h prior to analysis.

DNA encoding a firefly luciferase gene was targeted to the
AAVS1

Briefly, hPSCs were targeted by electroporation of 5 μg of each TALEN vector with 20 μg of the Luciferase containing targeting vector using a Biorad GenePulser (Hercules, CA) using an exponential decay and 250V and 500uF settings. Differentiation into pancreatic cells
To initiate differentiation, confluent cultures were dissociated into single-cell suspensions using TrypLE Select, counted, and seeded in 6-well suspension plates at a density of 5.5×10
6

The plates were incubated at 37°C and 5% CO2 on an orbital shaker set at 100 rpm to induce 3D sphere formation. After 24 hours, the spheres were differentiated as previously described (
Nair et al., 2019b

The resuspended spheres were distributed into fresh 6-well suspension plates for a final volume of 5.5 mL of day 1 media per well. Until day 3, spheres were fed daily by removing 5 mL of the media and replenishing with 5.5 ml. From days 4 to 20, 5 mL media was removed daily and 5 mL of fresh media was added. Media compositions are as follows: Day 1: RPMI (GIBCO) containing 0.2% FBS, 1:5,000 ITS (GIBCO), 100 ng/ml activin A and 50 ng/ml WNT3a (R&D Systems). Day 2: RPMI containing 0.2% FBS, 1:2,000 ITS and 100 ng/ml activin A. Day 3: RPMI containing 0.2% FBS, 1:1,000 ITS, 2.5 μM TGFbi IV (CalBioChem) and 25 ng/ml KGF (R&D Systems). Day 4–5: RPMI containing 0.4% FBS, 1:1,000 ITS and 25 ng/ml KGF. Day 6–7: DMEM (GIBCO) with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27 (GIBCO) and 3 nM TTNPB (Sigma). Day 8: DMEM with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27, 3 nM TTNPB and 50 ng/ml EGF (R&D Systems). Day 9–11: DMEM with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27, 50 ng/ml EGF and 50 ng/ml KGF. Day 12+: DMEM with 25 mM glucose containing 1:100 B27, 1:100 Glutamax (GIBCO), 1:100 NEAA (GIBCO), 10 μm ALKi II (Axxora), 500 nM LDN-193189 (Stemgent), 1 μm Xxi (Millipore), 1 μM T3 (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 mM vitamin C, 1 mM N-acetyl cysteine (Sigma-Aldrich),10 μM zinc sulfate (Sigma-Aldrich) and 10 μg/ml of heparin sulfate.

Dynamic perifusion assay for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion
Dynamic glucose-stimulated insulin secretion was performed using a perifusion system (Biorep technologies) as previously described (
Nair et al., 2019b

Immunostaining
Differentiated β-like clusters were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min at room temperature, washed with PBS, and stored at 4°C until ready for processing. β-like clusters were first embedded in 2% agar, followed by dehydration, paraffin embedding, and sectioning at 5 μm thickness. Paraffin-embedded sections were rehydrated in an ethanol gradient followed by incubation in slow boiling antigen retrieval Citra Solution (Biogenex). Spleen tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 2–4h, washed with PBS, followed by overnight incubation with 30% (w/v) sucrose (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS. Tissues were embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Tissue-Tek) and stored at −80°C before sectioning on a cryostat (Leica). Slides were briefly rehydrated in PBS before staining. For immunofluorescence staining, tissue was permeabilized and blocked in CAS block (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with 0.2% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) for at least 20 min, followed by primary antibody staining at 4°C overnight. Sections were washed with PBS-Tween 0.1% prior to secondary antibody staining performed at room temperature for 1h. Sections were washed again with PBS-Tween 0.1% before mounting with ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were acquired on an SP5 confocal microscope (Leica). Isolation of human PBMC
Human PBMC were isolated from fresh leukapheresis packs obtained from healthy donors (StemCell Technologies). Demographics and HLA class I typing for each donor is presented in
Table S2

Lentiviral infection
hPSCs differentiated up to day 14–15 were dissociated to single cells using Accumax. Digested cells were filtered on a 0.4 μm strainer and reaggregated in a suspension plate in the presence of lentiviral particles carrying a luciferase transgene (kindly provided by Dr. Audrey Hendley). Bioluminescence imaging
Mice transplanted with luciferase-expressing cells were injected intraperitoneally (IP) with 15 mg/mL D-luciferin solution (Goldbio Biotechnology) before imaging on a Xenogen IVIS 200 imaging system (Perkin Elmer). Signals were acquired and analyzed using the Living Image analysis software (Xenogen Corp). Regions of interests (ROIs) of the same size were manually drawn and bioluminescence was quantified as total flux (photons/sec). Background bioluminescence (determined using control mice not transplanted with hPSCs) was substracted from total flux values. Identical protocol was strictly followed for sequential imaging of the same mice to ensure comparability of assay performance over time.

Data for HLA-A*02 allele frequency in all populations and all regions of the world in studies that contained more than 1000 subjects was extracted.
